analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from requiring lenders to guess an applicant's race by appearance or surname.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on March 27, 2023, with 2 cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal agency from requiring a lender, when extending credit, to estimate a borrower's race or ethnicity by visually observing the borrower or by their surname. This targets a data-collection method regulators proposed for fair-lending enforcement — guessing a borrower's race when the borrower does not self-identify — which civil-rights enforcers use to spot discrimination in lending, but which critics say amounts to profiling and invades applicants' privacy.
analysis.who_benefits: Lenders, including banks and small business lenders, gain by avoiding a federal requirement to visually categorize applicants — an administrative and reputational burden. Borrowers also gain a privacy protection: no lender employee would be required to record a guess about their race or ethnicity without their say-so.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal agency from requiring a person or entity extending credit to estimate a borrower's race or ethnicity via visual observation or surname [S3].
Applicants would no longer face the possibility that a lender employee visually profiles them and records a race or ethnicity they never chose to disclose [S2].
Lenders would be spared a compliance task that would otherwise be imposed by federal regulation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fair-lending enforcement would lose one tool: the ability to compare lending outcomes for people whose race is estimated rather than self-reported, which is how regulators and researchers detect discrimination against minority-owned businesses and communities. Federal regulators' data-collection programs would be constrained.

drawbacks.text: The bill blocks a method regulators had considered for completing fair-lending data when applicants do not self-identify; without it, discrimination in small business and consumer lending can be harder to detect and prove, particularly for minority-owned businesses [S2].

The bill is narrow: it does not change what lenders may or may not do in deciding loans, and does not itself address lending discrimination — it only removes one federal data-collection requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine privacy and anti-profiling protection for applicants, but it is a narrow measure whose main practical effect is to relieve lenders of a data-collection duty. The cost — a weaker ability to document lending discrimination through borrower data — falls on enforcement efforts that minority borrowers and communities rely on. Both sides of the ledger are modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Roger Williams of Texas introduced the bill on March 27, 2023, joined by Representatives Luetkemeyer and Hill as original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and the complete action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The bill drew 2 cosponsors, both Republicans, and never reached the House floor [S4].
The CRS summary confirms the bill's single provision: prohibiting federal agencies from requiring lenders to estimate race or ethnicity by visual observation or surname [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, federal regulators kept their legal ability to require race and ethnicity data collection from lenders, and lenders did not get the statutory relief the bill offered. Neither side achieved anything; the privacy protection and the enforcement tool both remain exactly as they were.

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set its single provision barring agencies from requiring visual or surname-based race estimation in lending.

for.name: Reps. Blaine Luetkemeyer and French Hill
for.role: U.S. Representatives (MO, AR); original cosponsors on the Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Chair of the House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for any committee consideration; after its referral, the bill's action history shows no further steps [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no roll-call split exists; all three sponsors were Republicans and both cosponsors were Republicans [S4], and no recorded opposition appears in the record — the bill simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Banks, mortgage lenders, and small business lenders
industries.note: The bill would spare lenders a federal requirement to estimate and record applicants' race or ethnicity — a compliance burden for the industry, but also a data tool used to detect lending discrimination against minority borrowers. The industry's gain would come at the cost of fair-lending enforcement that serves the public [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Fair-lending data collection and civil rights monitoring
industries.note: Researchers and enforcers who use borrower demographic data to uncover discrimination in small business and consumer lending would lose one fallback method for completing records when applicants do not self-identify [S2].
